newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan bourse's future depends on polls - Habib.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan bourse's future depends on polls - Habib.

text.p: Karachi Stock Exchange (KSE) president Arif Habib, on Sunday linked the future of Pakistan's stock market to the February 3 general election.

President Farooq Leghari called the election after sacking Benazir Bhutto's government on disputed charges of corruption and misrule, and dissolving the National Assembly on November 5. He installed a caretaker cabinet to oversee the polls.

"How the market will behave in the immediate future will depend upon the initiatives of the interim government, the results of the elections in February 1997 and the policies of the elected government," Habib said in the KSE's annual report for 1996, which was released on Sunday.
The report, on the period from January 1 to October 29, said the KSE 100-share index had hit a low of 1,332.14 points on September 10 and a high of 1,855.22 on February 15.
Market capitalisation rose to 484.99 billion rupees on October 29 from 322.18 billion on January 1, the report said.
The number of listed companies on the KSE rose to 780 on October 29 from 764 on January 1. The KSE delisted 11 companies for violating KSE rules.
"This year has been a period of turmoil and change -- of anxiety and restlessness," Habib said.

"The political scenario has been marked by extreme tension. The structural weaknesses of the economy have been exposed and have become all too apparent. The chronic budgetary deficit has led to a harsh budget," he added.
Average daily turnover doubled to 28 million shares, while capital mobilised fell to 13 billion rupees from 30 billion.
"It is this weakness of the market that has been apparent for more than a year that is the major cause of concern," Habib said.
He said the KSE had approved the creation of an investors' protection fund to respond in the event of default by a member of the exchange.

The market had suffered because of over-valuation of shares of companies not yet in production. "The CLA has been persuaded to review the matter and it has now been agreed that no premium will be allowed on greenfield projects," Habib said.
The Central Depository Company could begin work two months after promulgation of an authorising ordinance. "This will mark the entry of our capital market into the modern age," he said.
